lesson.title: Breaking the Union: South Carolina's Gamble and the Deep South's Exit
lesson.summary: Beginning with South Carolina in December 1860, seven Deep South states seceded from the Union before Lincoln even took office, acting on the belief that a Republican administration threatened the survival of slavery.
lesson.body:
Secession did not spring up suddenly after the Election of 1860; it was the culmination of decades of sectional argument over slavery's expansion, states' rights, and the balance of power in Congress. What Lincoln's victory did was remove the last practical check Southern political leaders believed they had against a hostile national government. South Carolina, which had flirted with disunion as far back as the nullification crisis of the early 1830s, acted first and fastest. Its state convention voted unanimously to secede on December 20, 1860, less than seven weeks after the election, and issued a formal declaration of causes that named the election of a president hostile to slavery and the refusal of Northern states to return fugitive enslaved people as its central grievances.

Six more Deep South states followed within about six weeks: Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas had all seceded by February 1, 1861. Their public declarations of secession, where states issued them, spoke openly and repeatedly about protecting slavery, not primarily about abstract states' rights or tariffs, though those arguments appeared too. These were the states with the highest concentrations of enslaved people and the greatest economic dependence on plantation agriculture, and their leaders argued that a Republican administration, even one that promised only to stop slavery's expansion rather than abolish it outright, would eventually doom the institution by surrounding it with free states and territories.

The Upper South and border states, including Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas, held back through the winter of 1860 and 1861. Many voters and political leaders in these states hoped compromise was still possible, and several last-ditch efforts, including the Crittenden Compromise in Congress, tried to find a formula that might have restored the old Missouri Compromise line or otherwise protected slavery where it existed. None succeeded, in large part because Republicans, including Lincoln himself, refused to accept any deal that would allow slavery to expand into new territories, and because the seceding states were already moving to build their own separate government.

Outgoing President James Buchanan, whose term ran until March 1861, insisted that secession was illegal but also claimed the federal government had no clear constitutional power to force a state back into the Union, leaving the crisis largely unresolved when Lincoln finally took office. It would take the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861, and Lincoln's subsequent call for troops to suppress the rebellion, to push Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina to secede as well, bringing the total to eleven states and setting the geographic shape of the war that followed.
